title: Nine chores for three agents: complete EFX existence with an exact computational certificate
oneLine: Any nine indivisible chores can be shared among three agents with a strong fairness guarantee—even when their additive costs disagree and some chores cost nothing.
abstract: A computer-assisted candidate proof establishes complete EFX existence for three agents and nine chores with arbitrary nonnegative additive real costs, including deletion of owned zero-cost chores. A written reduction gives a canonical 21-variable counterexample domain; exact input reconstruction, rational Farkas certificates and reverse unit propagation refute it. The package includes a rational-input allocation finder, a general minimum-lowering lemma and a supplementary finite representative bound. It does not settle arbitrary chore counts or validate real-world cost elicitation.

problem.name: Three-agent EFX existence for nine chores

keyResults: Theorem 1: complete EFX allocation exists for every nonnegative additive real-cost instance with three agents and nine chores; every owned chore, including zero-cost chores, is covered.
Lemma 3: lowering one global minimum in each row to zero preserves nonexistence for any finite number of agents and chores.
The exact unbounded 21-variable counterexample formula is refuted by 370,780 rational arithmetic axioms and 172,146 RUP deductions.
For rational costs an exhaustive fixed-size finder returns an allocation with all 18 literal deletion comparisons; bit complexity depends on input size.
evidence: Written reductions and precise source dependencies; exact SMT input; complete selected arithmetic and Boolean proof objects; standard-library checkers and semantic controls; normal and optimized internal replay; exact allocation finder and worked example; manifest and AI index.

narration:
Three people have nine chores to share. They may disagree completely about which jobs are unpleasant. Can the chores always be divided with a strong fairness guarantee?

This Evidence Press candidate says yes, provided each person’s costs add across chores. The guarantee is called envy-freeness up to any chore. Remove any one chore from your own bundle, even a chore you consider costless. What remains must be no more costly, by your own standards, than either person’s entire bundle. It does not mean everyone receives the same number of chores, or that their total burdens are equal.

The proof first narrows any hypothetical counterexample to twenty-one real variables. There are nineteen thousand six hundred and eighty-three complete assignments. The formula handles assignments where everyone has at least one chore. A written argument covers the other assignments. Separate checking software checks each step of the contradiction, using exact fractions and elementary logical deductions. It does not simply accept a solver’s verdict.

The package also includes an allocation finder. Given rational costs, it returns a division and the eighteen inequalities that let a reader check it directly. The result extends an earlier eight-chore existence theorem. It does not settle arbitrary numbers of chores, strategic reporting or real-world measurement of inconvenience.

This remains an unrefereed candidate. Internal replay is not independent external reproduction, and the complete proof has not been formalised in a proof assistant. The paper, source code and proof objects accompany Nine chores for three agents, released on the eighth of October twenty twenty-six. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional mathematical evidence.
